intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that cerebellar ataxia, impaired intellectual development, and dysequilibrium syndrome-4 (CAMRQ4) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the ATP8A2 gene (605870) on chromosome 13q12.

checks.claim: Cerebellar ataxia, impaired intellectual development, and dysequilibrium syndrome-4 (CAMRQ4) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the ATP8A2 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Altogether, 6 of the 7 homozygous or compound heterozygous missense mutations known in ATP8A2 located in this subregion (amino acids 364‐877) of the catalytic cytoplasmic domain.
checks.explanation: Paper attributes CAMRQ4 to ATP8A2 mutations, citing homozygous and compound heterozygous cases.

checks.claim: The ATP8A2 gene is located on chromosome 13q12.
checks.evidence_quote: Homozygosity mapping revealed that several shared homozygous regions, including chromosome 13q12. Targeted next-generation sequencing of an affected individual followed by segregation analysis, population screening and prediction approaches revealed a novel missense variant, p.I376M, in ATP8A2.
checks.explanation: The gene's location at 13q12 follows from the mapped region; it is also standard nomenclature.

paragraphs.text: Cerebellar ataxia, impaired intellectual development, and dysequilibrium syndrome-4 (CAMRQ4) is an autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental disorder. Its features include cerebellar ataxia, hypotonia, intellectual disability, dysarthria and cerebellar atrophy, and some affected individuals have quadrupedal locomotion (Onat et al., 2013; Mohamadian et al., 2020). Severity varies widely. Some patients cannot sit or hold up their head and have involuntary movements and visual and hearing impairments (Narishige et al., 2022). Others learn to walk and have near-normal cognition (Damasio et al., 2021).

checks.claim: CAMRQ4 is an autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental disorder.
checks.evidence_quote: The pattern of inheritance in all of the possible phenotypes is autosomal recessive.
checks.explanation: The abstract also calls CAMRQ a rare, early-onset neurodevelopmental disorder.

checks.claim: Features of CAMRQ4 include cerebellar ataxia, hypotonia, intellectual disability, dysarthria and cerebellar atrophy.
checks.evidence_quote: three additional patients in an Iranian consanguineous family with non-progressive cerebellar ataxia, severe hypotonia, intellectual disability, dysarthria, and cerebellar atrophy have been identified.
checks.explanation: These features are listed for the patients and for CAMRQ4 in general.

checks.claim: Some individuals with CAMRQ4 have quadrupedal locomotion.
checks.evidence_quote: Missense mutation in the ATPase, aminophospholipid transporter protein ATP8A2 is associated with cerebellar atrophy and quadrupedal locomotion.
checks.explanation: The title links ATP8A2 mutation with quadrupedal locomotion.

checks.claim: The severity of CAMRQ4 varies widely.
checks.evidence_quote: These results allowed us to establish this as a disease-causing variant and expand ATP8A2-related disorders to include less severe forms of congenital ataxia.
checks.explanation: Paper implies a broader severity spectrum by extending to less severe forms, but does not explicitly state severity varies widely.

checks.claim: Some patients with CAMRQ4 cannot sit or hold up their head and have involuntary movements and visual and hearing impairments.
checks.evidence_quote: However, visual and hearing impairments associated with involuntary movements and severe developmental delay may be a clue to suspect CAMRQ4.
checks.explanation: Supported for these siblings, who could not sit or achieve head control and had involuntary movements and visual and hearing impairment. The draft generalizes this to 'some patients'.

checks.claim: Some patients with CAMRQ4 learn to walk and have near-normal cognition.
checks.evidence_quote: two siblings with congenital ataxia, who acquired independent gait by age 4 years. After 16 years of follow-up they presented near normal cognition
checks.explanation: The abstract reports this for only 2 siblings with congenital ataxia. It does not name CAMRQ4 or generalize to patients with the disorder.

paragraphs.text: Mohamadian et al. (2020) described 3 sibs from a consanguineous Iranian family of Arab descent: a 9-year-old girl (the proband), her 15-year-old sister and her 17-year-old brother. Their parents were healthy first cousins. The sibs had nonprogressive cerebellar ataxia, severe hypotonia, intellectual disability, dysarthria and cerebellar atrophy. The proband had severe neonatal hypotonia, global psychomotor delay and feeding difficulties from infancy. She was wheelchair-bound and could not walk, sit or hold up her head. All 3 patients had an IQ of 20 to 40, delayed speech with dysarthria, absent deep tendon reflexes, and cerebellar atrophy on brain MRI. Hearing was normal, there were no seizures or optic atrophy, and metabolic investigations were normal.

paragraphs.text: Narishige et al. (2022) reported 2 Japanese sibs with CAMRQ4 who developed athetotic movements at 1 and 2 months of age. They also had ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, feeding difficulty, hypotonia and severely delayed development. One sib had retinal degeneration and optic atrophy. Areflexia and flattening of auditory brainstem responses developed later. At last follow-up, neither patient could sit or control their head, although some nonverbal communication was preserved.

paragraphs.text: The transmission pattern of CAMRQ4 is autosomal recessive. Affected sibs in consanguineous families were homozygous for ATP8A2 mutations, and their unaffected parents were heterozygous carriers (Mohamadian et al., 2020; Damasio et al., 2021). Affected sibs born to nonconsanguineous parents were compound heterozygous (Narishige et al., 2022).

paragraphs.text: Gulsuner et al. (2011) studied a large consanguineous Turkish family with quadrupedal locomotion, mental retardation and cerebrocerebellar hypoplasia. Diffusion-weighted imaging and fiber tractography showed abnormalities of the cerebellum and corpus callosum, particularly atrophy of the superior, middle and inferior cerebellar peduncles. Structural MRI showed further morphometric abnormalities in cortical areas, including the corpus callosum, precentral gyrus and Brodmann areas BA6, BA44 and BA45. Homozygosity mapping linked the disorder to a 7.1-Mb region on chromosome 17p13.1-p13.3. Targeted sequencing of this region in 3 affected individuals and 2 obligate carriers identified a private homozygous missense mutation, P856L, in the WDR81 gene (614218). The mutation cosegregated with the disorder in the extended family. It lies in a highly conserved region of WDR81 between an N-terminal BEACH domain and C-terminal WD40 beta-propeller domains. WDR81 is predicted to be a transmembrane protein and is highly expressed in the cerebellum and corpus callosum, particularly in the Purkinje cell layer of the cerebellum. Gulsuner et al. (2011) noted that WDR81 was the third gene implicated in quadrupedal locomotion in humans, after VLDLR and CA8.

paragraphs.text: Mohamadian et al. (2020) studied 3 affected sibs from a consanguineous Iranian family with CAMRQ4. After a normal karyotype and chromosomal microarray, whole-exome sequencing identified a homozygous c.1339G-A transition (NM_016529.6) in exon 14 of the ATP8A2 gene, confirmed by Sanger sequencing. The mutation causes a gly447-to-arg (G447R) substitution at an extremely conserved residue in the ATP-binding (N) domain. It segregated with the disorder: the parents and 2 unaffected sibs were heterozygous, and 1 unaffected sib did not carry it. The mutation was absent from public databases and from 100 ethnically matched controls. Structural modeling predicted reduced protein stability and an altered ligand-binding pocket.

paragraphs.text: In 2 sibs with congenital ataxia, Damasio et al. (2021) used exome sequencing to identify a novel homozygous variant in intron 17 of the ATP8A2 gene, c.1580-18C-G. Bioinformatics tools predicted that it creates a new acceptor splice site. In a minigene assay in HEK293T cells, the variant construct used an alternative acceptor splice site and produced an aberrant transcript that retained 17 bp of intron 17. This inserted 4 amino acids and created a premature stop codon. The authors concluded that the variant was disease-causing.

(2013) found an ile376-to-met (I376M) missense variant in the ATP8A2 gene in the 4 affected members of a consanguineous Turkish family with CAMRQ, quadrupedal locomotion and cerebellar atrophy. paragraphs.text: Mohamadian et al. (2020) found a homozygous c.1339G-A transition (NM_016529.6) in exon 14 of the ATP8A2 gene in 3 sibs with CAMRQ4 from a consanguineous Iranian family of Arab descent. The mutation causes a gly447-to-arg (G447R) substitution at an extremely conserved residue in the ATP-binding (N) domain. It was found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. The parents and 2 unaffected sibs were heterozygous, and 1 unaffected sib did not carry it. The mutation was absent from public databases and from 100 ethnically matched controls. Homology modeling predicted severely reduced protein stability (FoldX ddG 7.94 kcal/mol) and an altered ligand-binding pocket next to the active site.
